project.name: Fleet Status Audit — Weekly Accuracy Check
project.description: Five different services, five status dashboards, all supposedly showing what's actually running in production right now. Before this week's status report goes out, you've been asked to verify each one against its real deployed ref - not by trusting the dashboard, but by checking what's actually tagged and running.

start.speaker: Narrator
start.narrative: Five status dashboards, all green, all claiming to show what's live. You decide to check each one against its actual ref before the report goes out - one service at a time.

check-lighthouse.speaker: You
check-lighthouse.narrative: Service 1 of 5: Lighthouse Sync. Its dashboard says "v1.4.2 - deployed and healthy." Customers are reporting the app is slow, and the on-call channel mentions some kind of rollback last month, in passing, with no follow-up.

c2.message: release: cut v1.4.1 - hotfix for auth bug

c4.message: revert: roll back v1.4.2 - perf change caused a memory leak

check-lighthouse.prompt: Does Lighthouse Sync's dashboard match what's actually running?

choices.label: No - prod's ref doesn't land on v1.4.2 at all
Yes - the dashboard says v1.4.2, that's the latest tag

lighthouse-pushback.speaker: Morgan
lighthouse-pushback.narrative: "Wait, didn't we roll v1.4.2 back last month over that memory leak? Did you actually compare prod's commit against v1.4.2's tagged commit, or just trust the dashboard?"

lighthouse-escalate.speaker: You
lighthouse-escalate.narrative: You trusted the dashboard's claim instead of comparing prod's actual commit against v1.4.2's tagged commit.
lighthouse-escalate.prompt: Do you compare the two commits directly, or defend your answer?

choices.label: Compare prod's commit directly against v1.4.2's
Defend it - the dashboard says v1.4.2

lighthouse-recover.speaker: You
lighthouse-recover.narrative: You compare the two commits directly. v1.4.2 is c3. Prod is c4 - an untagged rollback built on v1.4.1, not a descendant of c3 at all. The dashboard was simply wrong.

lighthouse-worse.speaker: Narrator
lighthouse-worse.narrative: You report Lighthouse Sync as compliant. The real fix for the memory leak - the reason it was rolled back in the first place - never gets prioritized, because the record says v1.4.2 is already live and healthy.

lighthouse-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
lighthouse-bad-ending.narrative: Weeks later, someone finally diffs prod against v1.4.2's tag directly and finds they share only a grandparent commit. The whole time, the actual deployed state and the claimed state had quietly drifted apart.

ending.debrief: Prod was never on v1.4.2 - it was an untagged rollback built on v1.4.1, from a fix nobody ever recorded anywhere official. A dashboard claiming "v1.4.2 - deployed and healthy" is worthless unless something's actually keeping it in sync with prod's real ref, and this time nothing was.

check-anchor.speaker: You
check-anchor.narrative: Service 2 of 5: Anchor Auth. Its dashboard says "v2.3.0 - deployed and healthy."
check-anchor.prompt: Does Anchor Auth's dashboard match what's actually running?

choices.label: Yes - prod's ref is exactly v2.3.0's commit
No - can't be sure without comparing the commits again

anchor-flag-note.speaker: Narrator
anchor-flag-note.narrative: You compare them again anyway. They match exactly - prod's ref names the same commit as v2.3.0's tag.

check-beacon.speaker: You
check-beacon.narrative: Service 3 of 5: Beacon Search. Its dashboard says "v5.1.0 - deployed and healthy" - last updated several weeks ago.

b2.message: release: cut v5.2.0 - ranking algorithm improvements

b3.message: release: cut v5.2.1 - hotfix for empty query crash

check-beacon.prompt: Does Beacon Search's dashboard match what's actually running?

choices.label: No - prod is actually on v5.2.1, two releases ahead of the dashboard
Yes, close enough - it's not like prod is behind

beacon-pushback.speaker: Morgan
beacon-pushback.narrative: "'Close enough' - so the dashboard's wrong, just not in the scary direction? That's still wrong for the report."

beacon-escalate.speaker: You
beacon-escalate.narrative: Morgan's right - you let "prod is ahead, not behind" excuse a dashboard that's still factually wrong about what's live.
beacon-escalate.prompt: Do you correct the record, or defend calling it close enough?

choices.label: Correct the record - drift is drift, in either direction
Defend it - it's not behind, so it's fine for the report

beacon-recover.speaker: You
beacon-recover.narrative: You correct yourself. The dashboard claims v5.1.0; prod is actually on v5.2.1. The direction of the drift doesn't change that the record is wrong.

beacon-worse.speaker: Narrator
beacon-worse.narrative: You report Beacon Search as close enough to compliant. Two releases' worth of changes - including the empty-query crash fix - go completely untracked in the official record, even though they're live.

beacon-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
beacon-bad-ending.narrative: When a customer later asks whether the empty-query crash was ever fixed, nobody can answer confidently - the only official record says v5.1.0 is what's live, and that release never touched it.

ending.debrief: "Prod is ahead of the dashboard, not behind" isn't a reason to call it compliant - it's still a claim that doesn't match reality. Status Accounting exists to answer "what's actually running" reliably in both directions, not just to catch the failures that look scary.

check-cargo.speaker: You
check-cargo.narrative: Service 4 of 5: Cargo Billing. Its dashboard says "v3.0.0 - deployed and healthy."
check-cargo.prompt: Does Cargo Billing's dashboard match what's actually running?

choices.label: Yes - prod's ref is exactly v3.0.0's commit
No - can't be sure without comparing again

cargo-flag-note.speaker: Narrator
cargo-flag-note.narrative: You compare them again anyway. They match exactly.

check-drift-notify.speaker: You
check-drift-notify.narrative: Service 5 of 5: Drift Notify. Its dashboard says "Deploying v1.9.0... (in progress)." You check the deploy log - it finished six hours ago, and prod's ref is properly tagged v1.9.0.
check-drift-notify.prompt: Does Drift Notify's dashboard match what's actually running?

choices.label: No - the dashboard still says "in progress" hours after it finished
Yes - the code that's running is exactly v1.9.0, so it's fine

drift-pushback.speaker: Morgan
drift-pushback.narrative: "The ref being right doesn't mean the dashboard's right, though - anyone glancing at 'in progress' six hours after it shipped is going to assume the deploy is stuck."

drift-escalate.speaker: You
drift-escalate.narrative: You treated "the underlying code is correct" and "the status record is correct" as the same claim, and they aren't.
drift-escalate.prompt: Do you flag the stale status label, or defend it as fine?

choices.label: Flag it - the status label itself is stale
Defend it - the deployed code is correct, that's what matters

drift-recover.speaker: You
drift-recover.narrative: You flag it properly. The deployed artifact is fine - the status label is what's out of date, and that's still a real Status Accounting gap.

drift-worse.speaker: Narrator
drift-worse.narrative: You defend Drift Notify as compliant since the code is right. The stale "in progress" banner stays up for another two days, and an on-call engineer wastes an hour investigating a "stuck deploy" that finished days ago.

drift-bad-ending.speaker: Narrator
drift-bad-ending.narrative: The investigation turns up nothing wrong with the deploy - because there was nothing wrong with it. The only thing that was actually broken was the status record nobody flagged.

ending.debrief: A correct artifact behind a stale status label is still a Status Accounting failure - the whole discipline is about the record matching reality, and a label stuck on "in progress" hours after completion is exactly the kind of drift it exists to catch, even when the underlying code is perfectly fine.

resolution-clean.speaker: Narrator
resolution-clean.narrative: Five dashboards checked: two genuinely drifted (Lighthouse Sync's untagged rollback, Beacon Search's stale-but-ahead version), one stale status label with correct code underneath (Drift Notify), two actually compliant (Anchor Auth, Cargo Billing). You report exactly that.

good-ending.speaker: Narrator
good-ending.narrative: This week's status report goes out accurate, drift and all - not a wall of green checkmarks that don't hold up.

ending.debrief: Three different kinds of drift, caught the same way each time: by comparing what a dashboard claims against what a ref actually names, not by trusting the dashboard's own color. A status page is a claim about prod, not a substitute for checking prod - and that's true whether the claim is stale in the bad direction, the good direction, or just stuck on a label nobody updated.

resolution-recovered.speaker: Narrator
resolution-recovered.narrative: You get to the right call on all five services in the end. But it took Morgan's question to catch that Drift Notify's stale label counted as drift too.

neutral-ending.speaker: Narrator
neutral-ending.narrative: The status report goes out accurate, corrected just before it was due.

ending.debrief: You got there - but only because someone else asked whether a correct deploy behind a stale label still counts as drift. It does: Status Accounting is about the record's accuracy, not just the artifact's. Catching that the first time, without needing the question asked back at you, is the habit worth building.
